candidate_sources.title: Phomopsis Tip Blight of Juniper (Phomopsis juniperovora) - Hort Answers - University of Illinois Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Phomopsis tip blight of juniper, caused by Phomopsis juniperovora (Diaporthe juniperivora). First symptom in spring is die-back of new shoot growth; new growth changes from light yellow-green to red-brown to ash-gray as it dies. Pycnidia produce conidia dispersed by air, rain splash, and insects. Plant resistant species, prune and burn blighted parts in dry weather, sterilize tools.

candidate_sources.title: Phomopsis Tip Blight – Wisconsin Horticulture
candidate_sources.snippet: Phomopsis tip blight is caused by the fungus Diaporthe juniperivora (formerly Phomopsis juniperovora). Disease occurs in late spring and fall when weather is cool and wet; succulent new branch tips are most susceptible. Small gray lesions form on terminal new shoots; infected branches turn dull red or brown then ash-gray as lesions girdle and kill tips. Management: prune in dry weather 4-6 inches below diseased areas, avoid overhead irrigation, plant resistant varieties, and apply fungicides such as copper, mancozeb, propiconazole, or thiophanate-methyl.

candidate_sources.title: Juniper Tip Blight - Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station (CAES)
candidate_sources.snippet: Juniper tip blight (Phomopsis juniperovora) fact sheet covering symptoms on new shoot growth, disease cycle, fruiting bodies (pycnidia), conditions favoring infection, and management including pruning, sanitation, resistant cultivars, and fungicide options.

candidate_sources.title: W1311 Phomopsis Blight of Juniper - University of Tennessee Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension publication on Phomopsis blight of juniper caused by Phomopsis juniperovora (Diaporthe juniperivora), detailing hosts (eastern red cedar and other junipers), symptoms, disease cycle, and integrated management.

candidate_sources.title: Kabatina Blight | Landscape, Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Kabatina blight, caused by the fungus Kabatina juniperi, primarily attacks and kills juniper twigs 1 year or older. This fungus does not infect healthy foliage, but enters through wounds caused by pruning, insects, or severe winter weather. Spores are formed in small, ash-gray lesions (cankers) at the junction between infected and healthy tissue.

candidate_sources.title: Kabatina and Phomopsis Tip Blight | Yard and Garden
candidate_sources.snippet: Kabatina tip blight symptoms appear earlier in the year, usually during February and March. Infected foliage turns pale green to yellow, then brown and dies. Small black dots, fruiting structures of the fungi that cause tip blights, are visible on the affected needles. Kabatina kills twigs 1 year or older, unlike Phomopsis which kills new spring shoots.

candidate_sources.title: Kabatina Tip Blight - MSU Extension | Montana State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Symptoms begin with the last 2-6 inches of branch tips turning a dull green that transitions into a red or yellow color, with gray to silver lesions developing at the base of the infected tip. The fungus overwinters in infected branches; spores cause new infections on at least one-year-old growth in the fall, with symptoms visible the next spring.

candidate_sources.title: Problem: Kabatina Tip Blight of Juniper - Kabatina juniperi
candidate_sources.snippet: Kabatina tip blight of juniper is caused by Kabatina juniperi. Dieback begins on shoot tips and progresses back toward the main stem; tips of affected branches turn yellow or brown. Management includes pruning out diseased tips during dry weather, improving spacing and air circulation, and avoiding wounding.

candidate_sources.title: Juniper Diseases & Insect Pests | Home & Garden Information Center
candidate_sources.snippet: Lophodermium juniperinum forms small, shiny, black elliptical fruiting bodies on the leaves and has been found many times over the years as a disease affecting juniper. Phomopsis blight (tip blight) most severely affects juniper species including eastern red cedar. Wet weather and poor air circulation, which keep foliage wet, favor disease development.

candidate_sources.title: Lophodermium Needle Cast : Landscape : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Spore-bearing structures appear as black, football-shaped lesions scattered along the center of the needle; symptoms first appear at the needle tips and slowly progress to the needle base, with dead needles lingering in the canopy into the next growing season. L. juniperinum can be regularly encountered on landscape junipers, especially prostrate cultivars. Management: remove dead stems/branches, especially in the lower canopy where Lophodermium can overwinter, and avoid prolonged leaf wetness.

candidate_sources.title: Juniper (Juniperus spp.)-Leaf Blight | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Juniper leaf (needle) blight on Juniperus spp. — pathogen, symptoms of foliar browning and needle cast, and management recommendations including pruning and fungicide options. Wet conditions and poor air circulation favor disease.

candidate_sources.title: Juniper Diseases | Penn State Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Overview of juniper diseases including tip blights (Phomopsis and Kabatina) and needle/leaf blights affecting Juniperus species, with symptom descriptions, causal fungi, and management practices such as pruning, sanitation, and avoiding overhead irrigation.

candidate_sources.title: Pestalotiopsis Blight | Plant Problems | Illinois Extension | UIUC
candidate_sources.snippet: Pestalotiopsis commonly causes a tip blight disease on conifers in the Northeast, Mid-Atlantic, Midwest, and Pacific Northwest. Junipers are frequently affected. Symptoms begin with needles turning green to yellow then brown, starting at branch tips. Pestalotiopsis is weakly pathogenic, colonizing stressed or wounded tissue. Management: prune dead/diseased tissue in dry weather, sanitize tools with 10% bleach or 70% alcohol, avoid crowding, copper fungicides in nurseries.

candidate_sources.title: Pestalotiopsis Tip Blight and Dieback, or Cryptomeria Blight / UC Statewide IPM Program (UC IPM)
candidate_sources.snippet: Pestalotiopsis tip blight and dieback (Cryptomeria blight) affects conifers including juniper, Leyland cypress, and arborvitae. Tips of branches turn brown to grayish; leaf spots are tan to gray, often following freeze injury, scorching, or mechanical wounds. Pestalotia is primarily a secondary, saprophytic pathogen that is weakly parasitic, infecting wounds under moist conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Pestalotiopsis disease: Causes & Control | RHS Advice
candidate_sources.snippet: Pestalotiopsis disease is common on outdoor ornamental conifers stressed after a tough winter or by wet soil. Pestalotiopsis species are weakly pathogenic, requiring a plant to be weakened or damaged to colonize it. Symptoms begin with needles turning green to yellow then brown, starting at branch tips; tightly grouped lower branches are affected first. Manage by pruning in dry weather and improving air circulation.

candidate_sources.title: Juniper: Phomopsis twig blight | Hortsense | Washington State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Phomopsis twig blight is caused by the fungus Phomopsis juniperovora. Symptoms include yellowing or browning of scales or tips of affected twigs on new and young needled foliage. Prune out and destroy blighted plant parts; sterilize cutting tools; avoid overhead irrigation and ensure good air circulation.

candidate_sources.title: Juniper Twig Blights | University of Maryland Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Juniper twig blights caused by the fungi Phomopsis and Kabatina are two of the most damaging diseases to junipers. The primary symptom of Phomopsis blight is browning and dieback of new shoot tips in spring. Small yellow spots appear on scale-like leaves; shoots fade to light green then reddish-brown and die back. Sunken dark lesions called cankers form at the junction of live and dead wood. The fungus overwinters on previous blighted twigs and bark.

candidate_sources.title: Juniper Twig Blight | Penn State Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Juniper twig blights caused by Phomopsis and Kabatina fungi cause dieback of shoot tips on junipers. Discusses symptoms, the disease cycle, and management practices including pruning and fungicide options.
